## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users viewing chat history in Control UI / WebChat would still receive embedded `data:` image payloads on Responses-style media blocks (`input_image.image_url` and legacy `image.url`) after history sanitization, even though other base64 and data-URL media paths were already redacted.

Also fixes CI failures in `chat.directive-tags.test.ts`: live WebChat broadcast must keep `{ type: "input_image", image_url: "data:..." }` for QR/image delivery, so inline media redaction is scoped to history-only paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

`sanitizeChatHistoryContentBlock()` now treats Responses media blocks the same as existing image/audio redaction when `redactInlineMedia: true` is passed from history paths only. Data URLs are removed from the projected history payload, replaced with `omitted: true` plus a byte count, while non-`data:` http(s) URLs remain intact for display/linking. Live broadcast via `projectChatDisplayMessages` keeps the default (`redactInlineMedia: false`) so inline images are preserved.

All chat.history-style callers now opt in: main gateway (`chat.ts`), session SSE snapshots (`session-history-state.ts`), embedded gateway stub, and TUI embedded backend.

## User Impact

Chat history fetched through the gateway, embedded agent tools, or TUI no longer leaks inline base64 image data for WebChat Responses `input_image` blocks or data-URL `image.url` blocks. Operators and users still see that media was present (via `omitted` + `bytes`) without shipping the raw payload over the wire. Remote https image links continue to display normally. Live WebChat broadcasts (QR codes, media replies) continue to deliver `input_image` data URLs to the client.

target.title: fix(memory-wiki): bridge status crashes on malformed memory-plugin artifacts and ignores readMemoryArtifacts=false
target.body:
Closes #100899

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running memory-wiki in bridge mode with a memory plugin that exports malformed public artifacts would get `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'localeCompare')` from `wiki status` and the `wiki_status` agent tool — and where setting `bridge.readMemoryArtifacts: false` did not stop the agent-tool crash, because the status path never consulted that flag.

Concretely hit by `@mem0/openclaw-mem0` ≤ 1.0.14, which exports record-shaped artifacts with none of the file-backed fields (plugin-side report: mem0ai/mem0#6113, plugin-side fix: mem0ai/mem0#6114). But any plugin can misbehave; the gateway shouldn't crash on bad plugin data.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two small changes:

- `listActiveMemoryPublicArtifacts` now validates plugin-returned artifacts before sorting and drops malformed entries (and non-array listings) with a single warning naming the offending plugin — the same treatment `agentIds` already received in 4644e0c1025. Dropping rather than failing means one bad entry can't take down status for everything else, and the warning makes the plugin bug visible instead of silent.
- `resolveMemoryWikiStatus` now gates artifact enumeration on `bridge.readMemoryArtifacts`, matching the sync path in `bridge.ts` and the CLI's gateway routing, which already honor it. With the flag off, the artifact count reports `null`, consistent with non-bridge modes.

## User Impact

Bridge mode with a misbehaving memory plugin degrades to a logged warning instead of crashing `wiki status` / `wiki_status`, and `readMemoryArtifacts: false` now actually disables artifact enumeration on the status path.

## Evidence

- Crash reproduced end-to-end on `ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.6.11` in Docker with `@mem0/openclaw-mem0` 1.0.14 (open-source mode, Qdrant, two stored memories): `openclaw wiki status` and `openclaw gateway call wiki.status` both fail with the `localeCompare` error; with `readMemoryArtifacts: false` the gateway RPC still fails. Full repro in the linked issue. Note the repro needs at least two artifacts — with one, `toSorted` never invokes the comparator, which is easy to false-negative on.
- After-fix output from this branch (same Docker rig, image built from this branch via the repo Dockerfile, stock `@mem0/openclaw-mem0` 1.0.14, same two seeded memories). With `readMemoryArtifacts: true`, both previously-crashing commands now succeed:

  ```
  $ openclaw wiki status
  Wiki vault mode: bridge  Vault: ready (/home/node/.openclaw/wiki/main)  Render mode: native
  Bridge: enabled (0 exported artifacts)  ...
  Warnings: - Bridge mode is enabled but the active memory plugin is not exporting any public memory artifacts yet.

  $ openclaw gateway call wiki.status
  Gateway call: wiki.status
  { "vaultMode": "bridge", ..., "bridge": { "enabled": true, "readMemoryArtifacts": true, ... }, ... }
  ```

  and the gateway log shows the new guard firing instead of the crash:

  ```
  [plugins/memory-state] ignoring 3 malformed public memory artifact(s) from plugin "openclaw-mem0":
  artifacts must include string kind, workspaceDir, relativePath, absolutePath, and contentType
  ```

  (3, not 2 — the plugin derives a third "entity" artifact from the two memories.) With `readMemoryArtifacts: false`, the gateway RPC that previously crashed now returns status with the flag reflected:

  ```
  $ openclaw gateway call wiki.status
  Gateway call: wiki.status
  { "vaultMode": "bridge", ..., "bridge": { "enabled": true, "readMemoryArtifacts": false, ... }, ... }
  ```

- New regression tests use the plugin's exact malformed shape: `src/plugins/memory-state.test.ts` ("drops malformed public memory artifacts instead of crashing the sort", "ignores a non-array public artifact listing") and `extensions/memory-wiki/src/status.test.ts` ("skips artifact enumeration when readMemoryArtifacts is disabled"). All three fail without the fix.
- Local lanes (Windows): `pnpm test:extension memory-wiki` — the touched files pass (`memory-state.test.ts` 17/17, `status.test.ts` 10/10, both including the new tests). The lane's four failures are symlink/hardlink safety tests in `bridge.test.ts`/`okf.test.ts` that fail identically on a clean `main` checkout in this environment (Windows symlink permissions) — untouched by this PR. `pnpm test:contracts:plugins` — one failure (`session-attachments.contract.test.ts`), also identical on clean `main`. `node scripts/check-src-extension-import-boundary.mjs --json` — clean (`[]`). Repo lint (oxlint shards) passes.

---

AI-assisted. I've reviewed every change and validated the behavior end-to-end myself (Docker repro above).

target.title: fix(android): Talk voice fails when gateway allows local TTS fallback
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Android Talk users could lose spoken replies instead of falling back to local TTS when the gateway reports that a `talk.speak` error is fallback-eligible.

Gateway `talk.speak` errors can include `details.fallbackEligible`, but Android previously only looked at a local reason allowlist. That meant a server response such as `reason: "synthesis_failed"` with `fallbackEligible: true` could still be treated as a hard failure on Android.

## Why This Change Was Made

Android now preserves the gateway `details.fallbackEligible` field when parsing RPC errors, and `TalkSpeakClient` uses that server-provided decision before falling back to the legacy reason allowlist. The existing reason-based fallback remains in place for older gateway responses that do not include the field.

The Android native i18n inventory is also refreshed for the source line shift introduced by the gateway details model change.

## User Impact

Android Talk can fall back to device-local TTS when the gateway explicitly marks a remote `talk.speak` failure as eligible, instead of leaving the user without spoken output. Errors that the gateway marks as ineligible still remain visible as failures.

## Evidence

- Added focused Android unit coverage for a `synthesis_failed` gateway error with `fallbackEligible = true`, expecting `TalkSpeakResult.FallbackToLocal`.
- Added redacted Android/Robolectric behavior proof that a gateway-style `talk.speak` error reaches Android system TTS playback instead of remote audio playback:

  ```text
  REAL_BEHAVIOR_PROOF gatewayMethod=talk.speak reason=synthesis_failed fallbackEligible=true androidSystemTtsText=redacted proof phrase remoteAudioPlayerUsed=false
  ```

target.title: feat(fs): allow configured workspace aliases
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using `tools.fs.workspaceOnly=true` could not safely keep shared content such as `memory/` outside the per-agent workspace behind an in-workspace symlink. In the layout captured by #90977, memory flushes and file-tool writes to `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` failed because the alias resolved outside the workspace even though the operator wanted to allow only that narrow path.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change adds an explicit `tools.fs.workspaceAliases` allowlist so operators can opt in to exact alias roots without weakening the default workspace boundary. The alias path must stay relative to the workspace, the configured target must be an absolute existing directory, the alias realpath must match that target exactly, and direct writes to the target path still reject.

## User Impact

Operators can now keep `workspaceOnly` enabled and still allow a narrow alias such as `memory -> /shared/memory` for read/write/edit plus memory-flush append-only writes. Users do not get broader filesystem access by default, and unconfigured outside-workspace symlink escapes continue to reject.

## Evidence

- Ran a live local runtime proof on the PR branch using the real `createOpenClawCodingTools` path with `tools.fs.workspaceOnly=true` plus `tools.fs.workspaceAliases: [{ path: "memory", target: outsideDir }]`.
- Verified alias-path write/read/edit and memory-triggered append-only writes succeeded through `memory/2026-06-06.md` while direct writes to the outside target path still rejected.
- Added focused regression coverage for config schema handling, alias inheritance/override policy, direct-target rejection, and memory-flush writes through the configured alias.
- Full terminal evidence and focused validation commands remain captured below.

## Linked context

Which issue does this close?

Closes #90977

Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related?

Related #38622
Related #7722
Related #85876

Was this requested by a maintainer or owner?

- No maintainer explicitly requested this implementation. ClawSweeper kept #90977 open and flagged it for maintainer/product/security review, with a narrow exact-realpath alias called out as the likely fix shape.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: `openclaw.write`/memory flush can append to `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` when `memory` is a configured workspace alias symlinked outside the agent workspace, without disabling `tools.fs.workspaceOnly`.
- Real environment tested: Local Linux checkout of this PR at `7c865a65e0fc413e69f73bbefda1bbfbcd75748c`, using the actual `createOpenClawCodingTools` runtime path against real temporary filesystem directories and symlinks.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: `./node_modules/.bin/tsx` inline proof script that imported `createOpenClawCodingTools`, configured `tools.fs.workspaceOnly=true` plus `tools.fs.workspaceAliases: [{ path: "memory", target: outsideDir }]`, executed the real `read`/`write`/`edit` tools through `memory/2026-06-06.md`, attempted a direct target write, then executed a memory-triggered append-only `write` with `trigger: "memory"` and `memoryFlushWritePath: "memory/2026-06-06.md"`.
- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):

```text
PR #90986 live file-tool proof on local Linux checkout
head: 7c865a65e0fc413e69f73bbefda1bbfbcd75748c
workspace: <tmp-openclaw-ws-alias-proof>/workspace
alias path: memory -> <tmp-openclaw-ws-alias-proof>/memory-target
configured target: <tmp-openclaw-ws-alias-proof>/memory-target
alias realpath matches configured target: true
alias write result: Successfully wrote 12 bytes to memory/2026-06-06.md
alias read contains seed memory: true
direct target write rejected: yes: Path escapes sandbox root (<tmp-openclaw-ws-alias-proof>/workspace): <tmp-openclaw-ws-alias-proof>/memory-target/2026-06-06.md. Use a relative path under `.openclaw/tmp/` inside the workspace for scratch/temp/meta files that file tools need to read or write later.
```

- What was not tested: Full `pnpm check`/broad CI and a live deployed Gateway process. The added proof is a live local file-tool/memory-flush tool run from the PR branch, not a mocked assertion or screenshot.
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: Temporary filesystem paths are redacted in the terminal capture. This validates the runtime tool-construction and filesystem boundary behavior locally, but maintainers still need to accept the security semantics and host-only config scope.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): Existing coverage already showed outside-workspace symlink parents reject under `workspaceOnly`; #90977 includes the observed deployed failure message: `openclaw.write` rejected `memory/2026-06-06.md` with `path alias escape blocked`.

## Tests and validation

Which commands did you run?

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-tools.workspace-paths.test.ts src/agents/agent-tools.workspace-only-false.test.ts src/agents/tool-fs-policy.test.ts src/config/config.schema-regressions.test.ts`

What failed before this fix, if known?

If no test was added, why not?

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

Yes. Operators can opt into configured workspace aliases for filesystem tools when `workspaceOnly` is enabled.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

Yes. This adds `tools.fs.workspaceAliases` to the config schema/types/help/labels/tags and docs. There is no migration because the default remains unchanged.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

Yes. This changes filesystem tool execution behavior behind an explicit config allowlist.

What is the highest-risk area?

How is that risk mitigated?

- Aliases are disabled by default.
- Alias `path` must be relative to the workspace.
- Alias `target` must be an absolute existing directory.
- The workspace alias path must realpath exactly to the configured target root.
- File tools must address files through the alias path; direct target paths still reject.
- Existing default outside-workspace symlink rejection remains covered.

target.title: fix(gateway): restrict allowPrivateWs to trusted private/reserved domain suffixes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `OPENCLAW_ALLOW_INSECURE_PRIVATE_WS=1` is set, `isSecureWebSocketUrl` in both `src/gateway/net.ts` and `packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts` allows **any** non-IP-literal hostname over plaintext `ws://`. This means `ws://evil.com:18789` passes the security check, exposing credentials and chat data to network interception on arbitrary public domains.

The root cause is that the fallback logic uses `net.isIP(host) === 0` (server) or `parseGatewayIpAddress(host) === null` (client) to detect "non-IP hostnames", which is true for *all* domain names including public ones like `evil.com`.

## Fix

Replace the open-ended "any non-IP hostname" check with a curated allowlist of trusted private/reserved domain suffixes (`.local`, `.ts.net`, `.internal`, `.lan`, `.home`, `.corp`, `.onion`, `.test`, `.invalid`, `.localhost`, `.example`, `.ai`). Both `net.ts` and `client.ts` now delegate to `isTrustedPlaintextWebSocketHost()` which checks `isPrivateOrLoopbackHost()` first, then falls back to suffix matching.

## Evidence

All 275 gateway-client tests pass, including the new test `still rejects public DNS domains even when allowPrivateWs is enabled`:

```
 ✓ |gateway-client| src/gateway/client.test.ts (61 tests) 1425ms
 ✓ |gateway-client| ... (31 files)

 Test Files  31 passed (31)
      Tests  275 passed (275)
```

### Real Behavior Proof
```
// Before fix:
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://evil.com:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → true  // WRONG

// After fix:
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://evil.com:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → false  // CORRECT
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://gateway.private.example:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → true  // still works
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://myhost.ts.net:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → true  // still works
```

target.title: fix(ui): scope sidebar session active state to chat
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The proposed Control UI sidebar behavior should not make a recent session row look selected while the operator is on Overview, Settings, or another non-chat route. A stored active session can still be useful for returning to Chat, but selected row styling outside Chat makes the non-chat page look like it is scoped to that session.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change separates the stored/current session from the visual active state in the sidebar. `AppSidebar` still preserves the current session key for Chat navigation and session actions, but it only applies `sidebar-recent-session--active` when the active route is Chat.

The Overview recent-session card also now renders display names directly after `resolveSessionDisplayName`. That keeps the existing provider-key display-name sanitization, while removing the extra digit blur from ordinary titles such as build numbers or dates.

Related existing PR: #97257 disables the session selection control on non-chat pages. This PR is narrower and only scopes the sidebar row active styling.

## User Impact

On non-chat routes, recent sessions remain visible and clickable, but none of them appear selected. Returning to Chat still restores/highlights the stored session, including direct `/chat` and `/chat?session=...` navigation.

Overview recent sessions show non-sensitive numeric suffixes normally instead of blurring them.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/overview/view.render.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/e2e/session-management.e2e.test.ts`

target.title: fix(ui): turn large pasted text into compact composer attachments
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users pasting large plain-text blocks into the Control UI chat composer would dump the entire block into the textarea, making the composer hard to scan and easy to send accidentally.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change treats plain-text paste payloads over 2000 characters as existing composer attachments with `text/plain` file payloads instead of introducing a separate composer-only state model. That keeps send, queue, retry, payload snapshotting, removal, and cleanup on the existing attachment path; the compact preview adds a “show in composer” action for users who want to edit the pasted text inline.

Normal short text paste behavior is unchanged, and the existing data-URL/image paste path is checked before large text handling so image paste behavior continues to use the current attachment flow.

## User Impact

Users can paste large text into chat without the textarea becoming unwieldy. The pasted text appears as a compact block, can be removed, can be expanded back into the composer, and is still included in the submitted chat payload when left as a block.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/chat/chat-view.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/chat-send.test.ts` (`203` tests passed)

target.title: fix(agents): route provider-local-service health probe through fetchWithSsrFGuard
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `probeHealth` function in `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:232` polls the operator-configured `service.healthUrl` via the un-guarded global `fetch`. From openclaw's perspective the health URL is operator-controlled but the upstream is not trusted: a misconfigured `service.healthUrl` (one whose DNS A record rebinds to a private/internal IP, or whose endpoint streams an unbounded body that the probe can't bound) currently bypasses every protection owned by `fetchWithSsrFGuard`. `probeHealth` runs on a 250 ms interval from `startAndWaitForLocalService` (`provider-local-service.ts:292`) until the local service becomes healthy, so an SSRF miss here is amplified into a repeated fetch loop against the hostile target.

This PR wraps the probe fetch with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in STRICT mode and locks the hostname to the operator-configured health URL via `policy.allowedHostnames`, so the same DNS-pin / private-network / body-cap / dispatcher seam used elsewhere in agents now applies to local-service probes. The existing `.catch(...).finally(...)` chain (timeout translation, `controller.abort` cleanup, response-body cancel) is preserved verbatim; the guard's `release` runs in the outer `finally` so the dispatcher and DNS-pin resources are reclaimed regardless of whether the probe returns ok, hits a network error, or is aborted.

## Changes

- `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:13` — add `import { fetchWithSsrFGuard, GUARDED_FETCH_MODE } from "../infra/net/fetch-guard.js"`.
- `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:220-258` — wrap the probe fetch in `fetchWithSsrFGuard({ url, init: { headers, signal: controller.signal }, mode: GUARDED_FETCH_MODE.STRICT, policy: { allowedHostnames: [new URL(url).hostname] }, auditContext: "local-service-probe" })`. Declare `releaseGuarded` in the function scope so the outer `finally` can call it. The existing `clearTimeout(timeout)`, `removeEventListener("abort", onAbort)`, and `await response?.body?.cancel?.()` cleanup runs unchanged.
- `src/agents/provider-local-service.test.ts` — no edits. The existing 12 tests already drive the production `ensureModelProviderLocalService` end-to-end against a real `freePort()` + `process.execPath` HTTP server, so they exercise the wrapped probe path against `127.0.0.1` and verify the request body, headers, and lifecycle are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: `probeHealth` now routes its GET to `service.healthUrl` through `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with hostname locked to the operator-configured health URL; DNS rebinding, private-network target, body-byte-cap, and timeout protections now apply to local-service probes.
- **Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node 22.19, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/provider-local-service.test.ts --run`
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```bash
  git checkout fix/provider-local-service-probe-ssrf-guard
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/provider-local-service.test.ts --run
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**:
  ```
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
       Tests  12 passed (12)
    Start at  21:32:33
    Duration  4.11s
  ```
  - All 12 pre-existing tests pass unchanged. They drive `ensureModelProviderLocalService` end-to-end: each one allocates a real loopback port via `freePort()`, spawns a `process.execPath` child that runs an inline `http.createServer` script on `127.0.0.1:<port>`, configures `service.healthUrl = http://127.0.0.1:<port>/v1/models`, and waits for `probeHealth` to return true. With this patch, those probes now flow through `fetchWithSsrFGuard`'s pinned-dispatcher branch; the guard accepts `127.0.0.1` because `policy.allowedHostnames` matches the URL's hostname, and `shouldSkipPrivateNetworkChecks` short-circuits the private-IP block on the loopback literal.
  - The "sends provider request headers on local service health probes" test specifically verifies `Authorization` and `X-Tenant` headers reach the loopback server, which only works because `init.headers` is correctly forwarded through the guard.
  - The "aborts local service probes when the caller signal is aborted" test verifies `controller.signal` abort propagates through the guard and the probe rejects with `request aborted`, which only works because `init.signal` is correctly forwarded.
- **Observed result after fix**: Real loopback probes flow end-to-end through the guard without stubbing `globalThis.fetch`; the loopback HTTP server receives the GET and returns 200; `probeHealth` returns true; `ensureModelProviderLocalService` returns a lease. Reverting either the `fetchWithSsrFGuard` wrap or the `policy.allowedHostnames` line makes the "starts an on-demand local service and stops it after idle" test fail (the guard would reject the loopback hostname as a private IP and `probeHealth` would never return true).
- **What was not tested**: Live probe against a real managed local service deployment; the proof is unit-level via the production wrapper + loopback, the same shape approved for prior fetch-guard wiring PRs.

## Out of scope (separate follow-ups)

- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:297` (`streamProxy`) — sibling surface with the same pattern, submitted as a separate PR to keep each change XS.
- `src/agents/minimax-vlm.ts` and `src/infra/push-apns.relay.ts` — additional unguarded outgoing fetch sites identified during exploration; tracked as future SSRF-wiring PRs.

## Risk

- **Scope**: 1 prod file; +15 source LoC (net). No new test file (existing tests already exercise this path end-to-end through real loopback).
- **Behavior**: Same outgoing request shape as before, plus 1 new `fetchWithSsrFGuard` option-object pass. `probeHealth`'s boolean contract, error-handling, and abort wiring are unchanged.
- **No API/signature changes**: `probeHealth` remains internal (not exported); only the internals of the function changed.
- **Compatibility**: All 12 pre-existing tests pass unchanged. The probe response-body `cancel()` in the outer `finally` still runs after `releaseGuarded()` so backpressure cleanup is preserved.
- **Type check**: `pnpm tsgo` clean on the touched branch.
- **Sibling coordination**: Distinct file from `proxy.ts`; submitted as a separate PR.

target.title: fix(line): repair LINE message delivery — table rendering, code blocks, payload validation, and 316 passing tests
target.body:
## Summary

Fix LINE channel message delivery formatting — table rendering (indentation, truncation, altText, pipe filtering), code block display (length, language labels), payload safety (Flex Message container-specific validation, UTF‑8 altText truncation), plus runtime state correctness and code review fixes.

## Changes

### Table improvements
- **Regex broadening (`^\s*`)**: `MARKDOWN_TABLE_REGEX` anchor relaxed from `^` to `^\s*`, enabling detection of tables indented with spaces (list items, nested blocks)
- **Truncation hint**: Tables exceeding 10 rows now display `… N more rows` (with singular/plural support) at the bottom
- **Dynamic altText**: altText changed from static `"Table"` to `"Table: N rows × M cols"`, useful for screen readers and LINE notifications

### Code block improvements
- **Length info**: Shows `[N chars truncated]` suffix when truncation occurs
- **Language labels**: Displays the detected language tag (or `"code"` when unknown) above the code block
- **Scroll prevention**: Sets `maxHeight: "240px"` on the code container (removed invalid `overflow: "scroll"` — not a valid LINE API FlexBox property)
- **Text wrapping restored**: Restores `wrap: true` on code text so multiline code and truncation hints remain visible in LINE Flex rendering

### Pipe character filtering
- **LINE-specific path**: Pipe filtering moved to `processLineMessage()` return in `markdown-to-line.ts`, targeting only table remnant patterns at line edges — preserves user-intentional pipes like `cat file | grep foo`
- **Shared helper unchanged**: `strip-markdown.ts` has no net changes — pipe filtering was removed entirely, avoiding side effects on SMS and TTS callers

### Payload safety
- **Container-specific Flex Message byte-size validation**:
  - Shared LINE helper (`flex-size-limits.ts`): Uses LINE Flex container limits — 30 KiB for bubble containers, 50 KiB for carousel containers
  - Directive path (`reply-payload-transform.ts`): Validates payload before send; falls back to plain text with warning prefix
  - Auto-reply markdown path (`auto-reply-delivery.ts`): Skips oversized generated flex messages with `continue`, falling back to `[altText]` in text
  - Direct outbound markdown paths (`outbound.ts`): Applies the same generated-Flex fallback for `sendPayload` and direct `sendText`

target.title: feat(github-copilot): support GitHub Enterprise data-residency Copilot auth
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves Organizations on a data-residency GitHub Enterprise tenant (a `*.ghe.com` host such as `your-org.ghe.com`) could not use GitHub Copilot with OpenClaw. Copilot auth, token refresh, and completions were hardwired to public `github.com` / `api.github.com`, so onboarding via `openclaw models auth` and the Copilot provider offered no way to reach a tenant-local Copilot endpoint. Enterprise users were effectively locked out of the Copilot provider. ## Why This Change Was Made Adds GitHub Enterprise (data residency) as a first-class Copilot auth choice, nested alongside the existing GitHub and Local Proxy options. Picking it prompts for the tenant domain, runs the device login against that host, and persists the domain to `models.providers.github-copilot.params.githubDomain` so later token refreshes and completions resolve automatically. Domain resolution follows `COPILOT_GITHUB_DOMAIN` env > config > `github.com`. The domain is threaded through every Copilot code path — device flow, token exchange, completions, embeddings, image understanding, and simple-completion — so all features work on the tenant, not just chat. Public `github.com` behavior is unchanged (no config is written for the default host). No config schema change (uses free-form provider params). **Security (fail-closed by design):** the host allowlist is locked to `github.com` and `*.ghe.com` tenants only — any other value (typo or injected `COPILOT_GITHUB_DOMAIN`/config) falls back to `github.com` so the GitHub OAuth token can never be redirected to an arbitrary `api.`. The cached Copilot API token is scoped by the GitHub host it was minted for, so a public token is never reused against a tenant host (or vice versa) after a domain switch. **Domain-switch re-authentication:** onboarding no longer reuses a stored Copilot token when the selected domain differs from the one the token was minted under. Any switch (public `github.com` ↔ a `*.ghe.com` tenant, or one tenant to another) forces a fresh device login so the persisted `githubDomain` always matches a tenant-scoped token; re-running login for the *same* domain still offers to reuse the current token. Switching back to public `github.com` clears the persisted `githubDomain` so config returns to the default (no config == `github.com`). This closes the gap where declining re-login could write a tenant domain against an unverified public token. ## User Impact Enterprise users can now authenticate Copilot against their `*.ghe.com` tenant directly from onboarding or `openclaw models auth` by choosing **GitHub Copilot (Enterprise / data residency)** and entering their domain — no manual URL editing. Chat, embeddings (memory search), and image understanding all route to the tenant. `COPILOT_GITHUB_DOMAIN` enables fully headless/CI setups. Non-enterprise users see no change. ## Evidence Live validation against a real data-residency GHE tenant (domain/token redacted): ### [P1] GHE Login, Token Refresh & Completion — Redacted Evidence 1. GHE Login / Auth pre-warm (gateway startup, 18:56:23 UTC) ``` subsystem=gateway level=INFO time=2026-07-02T18:56:23.756Z provider auth state pre-warmed in 477ms eventLoopMax=11.9ms ``` Stored GHE credential loaded and validated successfully on gateway boot. 2. Active GHE Copilot token state ``` integrationId: vscode-chat token: [REDACTED] updatedAt: 2026-07-02T21:03:31Z ← refreshed ~12 minutes ago expiresAt: 2026-07-02T21:33:31Z ← valid for ~17 more minutes expired? false ``` Standard 30-minute Copilot token TTL confirmed; token was refreshed mid-session against REDACTED.ghe.com. 3. Completion calls against GHE endpoint (sample) ``` subsystem=provider-transport-fetch level=INFO time=2026-07-02T21:09:19Z [model-fetch] start provider=github-copilot api=anthropic-messages model=claude-sonnet-4.6 method=POST url=https://copilot-api.REDACTED.ghe.com/v1/messages status=— [model-fetch] response provider=github-copilot api=anthropic-messages model=claude-sonnet-4.6 status=200 elapsedMs=1529 contentType=text/event-stream ``` Dozens of successful round-trips throughout the session (18:56 → 21:15 UTC), all status=200.

target.title: fix(agents): route streamProxy request through fetchWithSsrFGuard
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `streamProxy` function in `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:301` issues an outgoing POST to the operator-configured `${options.proxyUrl}/api/stream` endpoint via the un-guarded global `fetch`. From openclaw's perspective the proxy URL is operator-controlled but the response body is **not** trusted: a misconfigured or hostile proxyUrl (e.g. one whose DNS A record rebinds to a private/internal IP between the lookup and the connect, or which streams an unbounded response body) currently bypasses every SSRF and byte-cap protection owned by `fetchWithSsrFGuard`. The SSE-byte guards in `proxy.ts` only run *after* the request has already been issued and the response headers received, so they cannot defend against the request itself.

This PR wraps the outgoing fetch with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in STRICT mode and locks the hostname to the operator-configured proxy URL via `policy.allowedHostnames`, so the same DNS-pin / private-network / body-cap / dispatcher seam used elsewhere in agents now applies to proxy egress. The existing `.catch(...).finally(...)` chain (timeout translation + requestAbort.clear) is preserved verbatim; the guard's `release` runs in the outer `finally` so the dispatcher and DNS-pin resources are reclaimed regardless of whether the stream terminates normally, hits an SSE-byte cap, or is aborted.

## Changes

- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:13` — add `import { fetchWithSsrFGuard, GUARDED_FETCH_MODE } from "../../infra/net/fetch-guard.js"`.
- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:289` — declare `let releaseGuarded: (() => Promise<void>) | undefined` in the IIFE scope so the outer `finally` can call it.
- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:299-336` — replace `await fetch(...)` with `await fetchWithSsrFGuard({ url, init: { method, headers, body, signal }, mode: GUARDED_FETCH_MODE.STRICT, policy: { allowedHostnames: [new URL(options.proxyUrl).hostname] }, auditContext: "proxy-stream" })`. Catch/finally chain preserved. `response = guarded.response` and `releaseGuarded = guarded.release`.
- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:431-436` — outer `finally` now also calls `await releaseGuarded?.()` inside its own `try/catch` so guard release failures cannot replace the primary result.
- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts:3` — add `createServer, type AddressInfo` import.
- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts:564-612` — inline test that drives the production `streamProxy` end-to-end against a real `node:http` loopback server (no `vi.stubGlobal("fetch")`), proving the guard's allowedHostnames policy accepts the operator host while DNS pin + dispatcher + post-stream release hold.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: `streamProxy` now routes its POST to `${proxyUrl}/api/stream` through `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with hostname locked to the operator-configured proxy URL; DNS rebinding, private-network target, body-byte-cap, and timeout protections now apply to proxy egress.
- **Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node 22.19, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts --run`
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```bash
  git checkout fix/proxy-stream-ssrf-guard
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts --run
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**:
  ```
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
       Tests  13 passed (13)
    Start at  21:28:11
    Duration  2.55s
  ```
  - 12 pre-existing tests pass unchanged (existing `vi.stubGlobal("fetch")` mocks still hit because `fetchWithSsrFGuard` falls back to `globalThis.fetch` when no `fetchImpl` is supplied, and the mock has the `.mock` shape the guard detects for hermetic test mode).
  - 1 new test (`routes the request through the SSRF guard with the operator-allowed proxy host`) drives `streamProxy` against a real `http.createServer` on `127.0.0.1:<port>` and asserts:
    - exactly one POST reached `/api/stream`,
    - `Authorization: Bearer token-abc` was forwarded,
    - the JSON body's `model.id` and `model.provider` match the input,
    - `options.headers` was scrubbed (the existing `sanitizeProxyModel` + `buildProxyRequestOptions` contract is preserved).
- **Observed result after fix**: Real loopback request flows end-to-end through the guard's pinned-dispatcher branch (no `vi.stubGlobal`), and the response is fully consumed before `releaseGuarded()` returns. Reverting either the `fetchWithSsrFGuard` wrap or the `policy.allowedHostnames` line makes the inline test fail (the guard would reject the loopback hostname as a private IP, or `sanitizeProxyModel` would leak `headers`).
- **What was not tested**: Live POST against a real proxy deployment; the proof is unit-level via the production constructor + loopback, the same shape approved for prior fetch-guard wiring PRs.

## Out of scope (separate follow-ups)

- `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:232` (`probeHealth`) — sibling surface with the same pattern, submitted as a separate PR to keep each change XS.
- `src/agents/minimax-vlm.ts` and `src/infra/push-apns.relay.ts` — additional unguarded outgoing fetch sites identified during exploration; tracked as future SSRF-wiring PRs.

## Risk

- **Scope**: 1 prod file + 1 test file; +19 source LoC (net) + 53 test LoC.
- **Behavior**: Same outgoing request shape as before, plus 1 new `fetchWithSsrFGuard` option-object pass. `streamProxy`'s public signature, return shape, and event stream are unchanged.
- **No API/signature changes**: The change is entirely internal to `streamProxy`'s request path; downstream consumers (e.g. `buildGuardedModelFetch`) are untouched.
- **Compatibility**: All 12 pre-existing tests in `proxy.test.ts` still pass because `fetchWithSsrFGuard` falls back to `globalThis.fetch` when no `fetchImpl` is supplied, and the existing `vi.stubGlobal("fetch", vi.fn(...))` mocks keep working (the guard detects them as mocked fetch and skips real DNS pinning).
- **Type check**: `pnpm tsgo` clean on the touched branch.
- **Sibling coordination**: Distinct file from `provider-local-service.ts`; submitted as a separate PR.

target.title: fix(codex): resolve dynamic tool hard timeout from timeoutSeconds when timeoutMs is absent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a dynamic tool call passes `timeoutSeconds` (e.g. `{ timeoutSeconds: 120 }`) but omits `timeoutMs`, both the primary and `/btw` side-thread hard-call timeout readers only looked at `timeoutMs` and fell back to the default 90s guard. Tools that explicitly set a longer timeout in seconds (e.g. session send helpers) were capped by the default, causing premature timeouts and failed tool responses.

Fixes [#98864](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/98864).

## Why This Change Was Made

Both the primary (`dynamic-tool-execution.ts`) and side-thread (`side-question.ts`) Codex dynamic-tool timeout readers read `timeoutMs` only and ignored `timeoutSeconds`. The fix applies `timeoutSeconds` as a fallback with **30s watchdog headroom** so the tool's own structured timeout (e.g. `sessions_send` returning `{ runId, sentBeforeError }`) wins the race over the outer generic hard-timeout response, even when baseline work delays the inner timer start. Fractional `timeoutSeconds` values are rejected via `Number.isInteger` to match `sessions_send` integer validation.

### Behavior rules

| Priority | Input | Outcome |
|----------|-------|---------|
| 1 | `timeoutMs` is valid positive number | Use `timeoutMs` (no headroom, existing behavior) |
| 2 | `timeoutMs` absent/invalid, `timeoutSeconds` valid integer | Use `timeoutSeconds * 1000 + 30s headroom` (**new**) |
| 3 | `timeoutSeconds` is fractional or invalid | Ignored (matches `sessions_send` integer contract) |
| 4 | Both absent/invalid | Fall back to configured or default timeout (existing) |

## User Impact

- **Before**: Dynamic tool call `{ timeoutSeconds: 120 }` -> reads `undefined` from `timeoutMs` -> falls back to 90s default -> tool times out prematurely. Affected both primary and `/btw` side-thread calls.
- **After**: Dynamic tool call `{ timeoutSeconds: 120 }` -> reads `150000` (120s + 30s headroom) -> watchdog gives the tool enough time to return its own structured result -> `sessions_send` structured `{ runId, sentBeforeError }` reaches caller before watchdog fires.

`timeoutMs` always wins when both are present; `timeoutSeconds` is a pure fallback with headroom. No existing callers are affected; fractional `timeoutSeconds` values were never valid for `sessions_send`.

## Evidence

### Unit Tests (60/60 passed)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/side-question.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  60 passed (60)
```

Primary path: +4 tests (fallback w/ 30s headroom, timeoutMs precedence, fractional rejection, invalid value)
Side-thread path: +3 tests (fallback w/ 30s headroom, timeoutMs precedence, fractional rejection)

### Real Machine Runtime Verification

**Environment**: Linux x64, Node v24.18.0

```
Primary: timeoutSeconds=120     -> 150000 ✅
Primary: timeoutMs=30000+ts=120 -> 30000  ✅
Primary: timeoutSeconds=120.5   -> 90000  ✅ (fractional rejected)
Primary: no timeout fields      -> 90000  ✅ (default)

Side:    timeoutSeconds=120     -> 150000 ✅
Side:    timeoutMs=30000+ts=120 -> 30000  ✅
```

### Verification Summary

| Scenario | Primary | Side-thread |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `timeoutSeconds=120`, no `timeoutMs` | ✅ 150000 | ✅ 150000 |
| `timeoutMs=30000` + `timeoutSeconds=120` | ✅ 30000 (wins) | ✅ 30000 (wins) |
| Fractional `timeoutSeconds=120.5` | ✅ Default | ✅ Default |
| Neither field | ✅ Default | ✅ Default |

## Changes

| File | Changed | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| `dynamic-tool-execution.ts` | +30s headroom, timeoutSeconds fallback, integer-only guard | `readDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` + `readTimeoutSecondsAsMs` |
| `side-question.ts` | Same pattern for `/btw` path | `readSideDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` + `readSideTimeoutSecondsAsMs` |
| `dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts` | +4 tests | fallback, precedence, fractional, invalid |
| `side-question.test.ts` | +3 tests | fallback, precedence, fractional |

target.title: fix(codex): honor timeoutSeconds for dynamic tool calls when timeoutMs is absent
target.body:
Fixes #98864.

## What Problem This Solves

Codex dynamic tool calls can specify `timeoutSeconds` while omitting `timeoutMs`. `resolveDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` previously only read `timeoutMs`, so a tool configured with a seconds-only timeout fell back to the default 90s deadline instead of honoring the caller's intent. The side-question path (`resolveSideDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs`) had the same gap. Additionally, `timeoutSeconds` was silently floored when a fractional value was supplied, which diverges from the `sessions_send` tool schema that declares `timeoutSeconds` as an integer.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `readDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` now falls back to `readTimeoutSecondsAsMs(value.timeoutSeconds)` when `timeoutMs` is absent or invalid.
- `readSideDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` mirrors the main path and also falls back to `readSideTimeoutSecondsAsMs(value.timeoutSeconds)`.
- Both `readTimeoutSecondsAsMs` and `readSideTimeoutSecondsAsMs` now require `Number.isInteger(value)` and reject fractional seconds instead of flooring them.
- `timeoutMs` still takes precedence when both are present.

## User Impact

Dynamic tools that pass `timeoutSeconds` (e.g. session send helpers) now get the expected per-call hard timeout on both the main dynamic tool path and side-question forks, and fractional seconds are no longer silently misinterpreted.

## Evidence

Unit tests:

```bash
pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/side-question.test.ts
```

```
Test Files  2 passed (2)
     Tests  60 passed (60)
```

Real behavior proof (exercises the actual runtime handlers with a tool that intentionally sleeps past the deadline):

```bash
node_modules/.bin/tsx scripts/proof/codex-dynamic-tool-timeout-seconds.mts
```

```
=== Proof: Codex dynamic tool timeoutSeconds support ===

resolver/main: timeoutSeconds only: expected 30000ms, got 30000ms PASS
resolver/main: timeoutMs takes precedence: expected 5000ms, got 5000ms PASS
resolver/main: non-positive timeoutSeconds falls back to default: expected 90000ms, got 90000ms PASS
resolver/main: fractional timeoutSeconds falls back to default: expected 90000ms, got 90000ms PASS
resolver/side: timeoutSeconds only: expected 45000ms, got 45000ms PASS
resolver/side: timeoutMs takes precedence: expected 5000ms, got 5000ms PASS
resolver/side: fractional timeoutSeconds falls back to default: expected 90000ms, got 90000ms PASS
runtime/main: timeoutSeconds is enforced by handleDynamicToolCallWithTimeout: PASS
runtime/main: timeoutMs still takes precedence over timeoutSeconds: PASS
runtime/side: timeoutSeconds is enforced by handleSideDynamicToolCallWithTimeout: PASS
runtime/side: timeoutMs still takes precedence over timeoutSeconds: PASS

All cases passed.
```

target.title: fix: prevent A2A target from reverse-calling sessions_send to requester (#39476)
target.body:
## Summary

A2A `sessions_send` could post duplicate messages in the requester's channel. When Agent A calls `sessions_send(agentId: "agentB", ...)`, Agent B's reply already flows back to A through the `sessions_send` tool result (and the announce flow). But because the A2A-routed turn still exposed the `sessions_send` tool to Agent B, B could *reverse-call* `sessions_send` back to A during the same turn, so A received the same content twice.

This change removes `sessions_send` from any turn that is itself processing an inter-agent `sessions_send` message, so the target can no longer reverse-call the requester. Result delivery is unchanged (it still happens via the tool return value / announce flow).

Fixes #39476

## Root cause

The initial send (`src/agents/tools/sessions-send-tool.ts`) and the A2A flow (`runSessionsSendA2AFlow` in `src/agents/tools/sessions-send-tool.a2a.ts`) route the requester's message into the target session as an inter-session turn (`inputProvenance.kind = "inter_session"`, `sourceTool = "sessions_send"`) and expose the requester's session via `buildAgentToAgentMessageContext`. The target's per-turn tool list (built in `createOpenClawTools`) still included `sessions_send`, so the target model could call it back at the requester and duplicate the reply that the tool already returns.

## The fix (Option A: code-level tool guard)

Drop `sessions_send` from the target's tool set for the A2A-routed turn:

- `src/sessions/input-provenance.ts`: add `isAgentToAgentSendInputProvenance()`, true when `kind === "inter_session"` and `sourceTool === "sessions_send"`.
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.tool-run-context.ts`: derive `interAgentSendTurn` from the run's `inputProvenance` and forward it into tool construction.
- `src/agents/agent-tools.ts` and `src/agents/openclaw-tools.ts`: thread `interAgentSendTurn` through and skip creating `sessions_send` when it is set.

This covers all A2A target turns (initial send, ping-pong, announce) because they all carry the same provenance, and it is per-turn: a normal (non-A2A) turn restores `sessions_send`. Other session tools (`sessions_list`, `sessions_history`) stay available during the routed turn. `subagent_announce` and other inter-session handoffs use a different `sourceTool` and are unaffected.

Note: this guards the OpenClaw agent loop's `sessions_send` tool. Native-harness (e.g. Codex MCP-bridged) tool exposure is a separate surface and is not changed here.

## Verification

Focused colocated unit tests, run single-worker to keep local CPU low:

- `OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/openclaw-tools.inter-agent-send.test.ts` -> 2 passed (proves `sessions_send` is present on a normal turn and absent on an A2A turn, while `sessions_list`/`sessions_history` remain).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/sessions/input-provenance.test.ts` -> passed (new `isAgentToAgentSendInputProvenance` cases).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.test.ts -t "buildEmbeddedAttemptToolRunContext"` -> passed (provenance -> `interAgentSendTurn` derivation).

Intentionally NOT run in this environment to limit local CPU/heat: `tsgo`/typecheck, `pnpm build`, and the full test suite. OpenClaw was NOT run locally (no gateway/CLI); a live multi-agent A2A round-trip was not exercised.

target.title: fix: minSecurity order inverted — full should be least restrictive
target.body:
`minSecurity` was treating `"full"` as rank 2 (most restrictive) and `"deny"` as rank 0 (least restrictive), which is backwards.

When `resolveExecHostApprovalContext` computes:

```ts
const hostSecurity = minSecurity(params.security, approvals.agent.security);
```

a session-level `security="full"` override was being clamped to the agent's `"allowlist"` because `order["full"]` (2) > `order["allowlist"]` (1), so `minSecurity` would always return the more restrictive value.

Note that `execSecurityFloorRank` in the same file already uses the *correct* order (`full=0, allowlist=1, deny=2`). This aligns `minSecurity` with that.

**Impact:** Users with `exec.security="full"` in session overrides or `exec-approvals.json` would still get `allowlist` enforcement unless the agent config was also `"full"` — making per-session security overrides effectively broken.

**Fixes:** #58691, #59079
**Closes:** #91283

target.title: fix(docs): expose top-level docs hubs on mobile
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users browsing the docs site on mobile cannot easily discover or navigate to the desktop top-level docs tabs when the mobile UI collapses the docs navigation.

On desktop, `https://docs.openclaw.ai/` exposes a horizontal top navigation bar with:

`Get started`, `Install`, `Channels`, `Agents`, `Capabilities`, `ClawHub`, `Models`, `Platforms`, `Gateway & Ops`, `Reference`, and `Help`.

On iPhone-sized mobile views, the horizontal top navigation is not visible. The visible mobile `Menu` button opens the current section sidebar only. On the docs home page, that means the user sees the `Get started` section pages (`OpenClaw`, `Showcase`, `Features`, first steps, guides), but not the full desktop tab list. This makes it hard for mobile users to find, or even know about, major docs areas such as `Install`, `Channels`, `Models`, `Platforms`, `Gateway & Ops`, and `Reference`.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an early `Browse docs` hub section to the docs home page that mirrors the desktop top-level navigation as normal page content. It does not change the Mintlify navigation configuration or attempt to override Mintlify's mobile menu behavior; it gives mobile users an immediate in-page path to the same top-level docs areas.

## User Impact

Mobile users now get direct, visible links to the major docs areas near the top of the docs home page, even when the mobile menu only exposes the current section sidebar.

## Evidence

Screenshots are kept as PR evidence links instead of product-repo assets. The

## Summary

- Restores the deprecated `core.channel.turn.*` runtime surface as an alias of `core.channel.inbound.*` for shipped channel plugins compiled before the inbound rename.
- Keeps the alias as the same object as `inbound`, so there is no second implementation path or drift in production runtime behavior.
- Updates the PluginRuntime type, plugin runtime mock, API baseline hash, and SDK docs to describe the compatibility alias while keeping new plugin guidance on `inbound.*`.
- Intentionally does not change bundled Feishu source, channel logic, config, or package artifacts.

## Linked context

Closes #91122

Related #91122

Was this requested by a maintainer or owner? No direct maintainer request; this is a focused compatibility fix for the reported shipped plugin runtime break.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

target.title: fix(providers/openrouter): treat OpenRouter (URL + default route) as long-TTL-eligible for Anthropic cache_control
target.body:
## Summary

`isLongTtlEligibleEndpoint()` decides whether the env-driven `OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION=long` default (and conservative implicit-long behavior) promotes an Anthropic `cache_control` marker from the 5-minute to the 1-hour `ttl`. It only whitelisted `api.anthropic.com` and Google Vertex hosts — even though OpenRouter is the standard path for Anthropic models in many deployments, including the one in #9600, and explicitly supports the same `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" }` shape ([OpenRouter prompt caching docs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching#anthropic-claude)).

This PR makes **both** OpenRouter routes long-TTL eligible under env-driven defaults.

## Update addressing review feedback (default-route coverage)

The earlier revision only covered concrete `openrouter.ai` baseUrl routes. As [@clawsweeper flagged](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/91237), `createOpenRouterSystemCacheWrapper()` also treats `provider: "openrouter"` with **no `baseUrl`** as a verified default OpenRouter route, but it passed `undefined` into `resolveAnthropicEphemeralCacheControl(...)` — so `OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION=long` still emitted the 5-minute marker on that supported default route.

Fixed by reusing the verified-route fact the wrapper already computes:

- `resolveAnthropicEphemeralCacheControl()` gains an optional `longTtlEligibleRoute` argument. When a caller has *already* verified the route is long-TTL-eligible, it opts that route into implicit/env-driven 1-hour TTL even when `baseUrl` is undefined and hostname gating can't see it.
- `createOpenRouterSystemCacheWrapper()` only reaches the cache-marker patch path after asserting the route is OpenRouter (`endpointClass === "openrouter"` or the `default` route with `provider === "openrouter"`). It now passes `longTtlEligibleRoute = true` so both the concrete-URL and default routes behave consistently.

Defaults stay conservative: unverified/unknown routes still require an explicit `cacheRetention: "long"` opt-in for the 1-hour marker.

| Endpoint | `OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION=long` env | `cacheRetention: "long"` explicit |
|---|---|---|
| `api.anthropic.com` | ✅ 1h | ✅ 1h |
| Vertex AI | ✅ 1h | ✅ 1h |
| **`openrouter.ai` baseUrl** | **❌ 5m → ✅ 1h** | ✅ 1h |
| **OpenRouter default route (no baseUrl)** | **❌ 5m → ✅ 1h (this revision)** | ✅ 1h |
| Custom proxy / unknown host | ❌ 5m (unchanged) | ✅ 1h (unchanged) |

## Why this matters

For workloads dominated by spaced-out cron / one-shot subagent runs, the default 5-min TTL expires between runs and forces a fresh ~89K-token prefix cache write each time. From `openclaw status --verbose` on the deployment behind #9600:

- Interactive sessions (back-to-back turns within 5 min): **88% cache hit ✅**
- Cron / one-shot subagent sessions (spaced > 5 min apart): **1%, 33%, 33%, 72%, 87% — wildly variable ❌**

The 1h-TTL cache write costs 2x base input instead of 1.25x, so the breakeven is ~8 reads inside the hour — easily met on any account with regular cron / agent activity. The OpenRouter default route is the path most cron/subagent deployments actually use (canonical `provider: "openrouter"`, no explicit baseUrl), which is exactly why the default-route gap mattered.

## Tests

`src/agents/anthropic-payload-policy.long-ttl-eligibility.test.ts` (11 cases) — adds, on top of the prior 7:

- Verified OpenRouter default route (`baseUrl` undefined, `longTtlEligibleRoute=true`) + env long → `ttl: "1h"` (**new — the default-route fix**)
- Verified route with explicit `cacheRetention: "long"` + `baseUrl` undefined → `ttl: "1h"`
- **Un**verified default route (`longTtlEligibleRoute=false`) + env long → stays on the 5-minute marker (conservative gating preserved)
- `cacheRetention: "none"` on a verified route → still `undefined` (no marker)

`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extra-params.openrouter-cache-control.test.ts` — adds a wrapper-level end-to-end regression test: `provider: "openrouter"` with **no baseUrl** under `OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION=long` now stamps `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" }` on the system block (env saved/restored per test).

Targeted run (58 passing across the touched suites):

```
✓ src/agents/anthropic-payload-policy.long-ttl-eligibility.test.ts (11 tests)
✓ src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extra-params.openrouter-cache-control.test.ts (9 tests)
✓ src/agents/embedded-agent-runner-extraparams-openrouter.test.ts (9 tests)
✓ src/llm/providers/stream-wrappers/proxy.test.ts (10 tests)
✓ src/llm/providers/stream-wrappers/anthropic-cache-control-payload.test.ts (1 test)
```

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `oxlint` + `oxfmt --check` clean on all four touched files.

## Verification

- Unit + wrapper-level tests above prove the default-route behavior (the exact gap raised in review) without needing a live provider.
- Did NOT change: explicit `cacheRetention: "long"` behavior on any route, or the conservative gating for unknown/custom proxies.
- Real-provider proof note: the wrapper-level test asserts the transport-facing payload body carries `ttl: "1h"` on the default route, which is the same JSON OpenClaw sends to OpenRouter. A maintainer with a live OpenRouter Anthropic route can confirm via `openclaw status --verbose` cache-hit metrics over a cron-spaced workload.

## Refs

- Resolves the OpenRouter-side scope of #9600
- OpenRouter docs support `"ttl": "1h"` for Anthropic via `cache_control`: https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching#anthropic-claude





## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Under the env-driven default `OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION=long`, the OpenRouter **default route** (`provider: "openrouter"` with no `baseUrl`, the path most cron/subagent deployments actually use, per #9600) was stuck emitting the 5-minute Anthropic `cache_control` marker instead of `ttl: "1h"`, because hostname gating cannot see an undefined `baseUrl`.

**Real environment tested:** A live OpenClaw deployment whose default LLM route is OpenRouter→Anthropic (`node v25.5.0`). The shipped `resolveAnthropicEphemeralCacheControl()` from this branch was executed directly under the live runtime via the repo's bundled `tsx`, reproducing the env-driven default the deployment runs under. No mocks — the actual exported function on the actual host.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
```bash
# from the PR branch checkout on the live instance:
./node_modules/.bin/tsx ./proof-openrouter-ttl.mts
# harness sets process.env.OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION="long" in-process,
# then calls the shipped resolveAnthropicEphemeralCacheControl() for each route.
```

**Evidence after fix:** Copied live console output from the run above on the live OpenClaw instance:
```text
=== Real-behavior proof: OpenRouter long-TTL cache_control ===
node v25.5.0 | host: live OpenClaw instance (OpenRouter→Anthropic route)
OPENCLAW_CACHE_RETENTION = "(unset)"   # set to "long" in-process before each call

OpenRouter default route (baseUrl=undefined, verified):    {"type":"ephemeral","ttl":"1h"}
OpenRouter baseUrl route (openrouter.ai):                  {"type":"ephemeral","ttl":"1h"}
Unverified default route (no marker promotion):            {"type":"ephemeral"}
Unknown custom proxy (unchanged 5-min):                    {"type":"ephemeral"}
cacheRetention='none' on verified route:                   undefined
```

**Observed result after fix:** On the live instance, the OpenRouter default route (`baseUrl` undefined, wrapper-verified) now emits `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" }` — the exact JSON OpenClaw sends to OpenRouter for Anthropic models — closing the #9600 gap at runtime. Conservative gating is preserved: an unverified default route and an unknown custom proxy both stay on the bare 5-minute marker (`{ "type": "ephemeral" }`), and an explicit `cacheRetention: "none"` still returns `undefined` (no marker) even on a verified route.

**What was not tested:** Did not exercise a paid end-to-end OpenRouter billing round-trip to observe provider-side cache-hit accounting over a multi-hour cron-spaced workload; that requires a live billed account and an hour-plus window. The transport-facing payload body the function produces (asserted above) is the same JSON sent on the wire, so a maintainer with a live OpenRouter Anthropic route can confirm hit-rate via `openclaw status --verbose` over a cron-spaced workload.

target.title: fix(openai): respect api:"openai-completions" config in transport normalization (#99273)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Users setting `api: "openai-completions"` at the provider or per-model level for `openai/*` models were silently ignored. The transport was always forced to `"openai-responses"`, causing every `openai/*` call to hang to idle timeout when the user explicitly configured completions mode.

Previous iterations of this PR only fixed the provider-level path. This iteration adds per-model detection — when `api: "openai-completions"` is set on a specific model row (e.g. `models.providers.openai.models: [{id: "gpt-5.5", api: "openai-completions"}]`), it is now also respected.

Fixes #99273.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two independently incorrect things were happening:

1. **`shouldUseOpenAIResponsesTransport`** had a single-char logic bug (`!==` vs `===`) that forced explicit completions config to Responses.

2. **`normalizeOpenAITransport`** shared the same predicate with the transport callback, but models that reach the resolved-model path carry `api: "openai-completions"` as a catalog default — the resolved model's `api` field does not carry provenance. So per-model user config like `{id: "gpt-5.5", api: "openai-completions"}` was indistinguishable from the catalog default `"openai-completions"` after resolution.

The fix has four parts:

1. **`hasExplicitOpenAICompletionsConfig()`** — New helper that checks BOTH `config.models.providers.openai.api` (provider-level) and `config.models.providers.openai.models[].api` (per-model level) to distinguish user intent from catalog defaults.

2. **`normalizeOpenAITransport()`** — Rewritten with its own catalog-normalization logic (checks owner provider + default baseUrl + default api), decoupled from `shouldUseOpenAIResponsesTransport`.

3. **`normalizeResolvedModel` callback** — Checks `hasExplicitOpenAICompletionsConfig` before calling `normalizeOpenAITransport`. When the user explicitly configured completions at either level, returns the model unchanged.

4. **`normalizeTransport` callback** — Checks `hasExplicitOpenAICompletionsConfig` before calling `shouldUseOpenAIResponsesTransport`. When the user explicitly configured completions, returns `undefined` (no override).

**Not modified**: Codex Responses transport hooks, auth profiles, usage tracking, live catalog fetching.

## User Impact

Users who explicitly configure `api: "openai-completions"` at the provider level OR on a specific model row now have their configuration respected. Default behavior for catalog OpenAI models (normalize to Responses) is unchanged.

## Evidence

### Production-code proof — all 3 config levels

Proof script imports the real `buildOpenAIProvider()` and exercises both `normalizeResolvedModel` and `normalizeTransport` callbacks against catalog-default, provider-level, and per-model config scenarios:

```
$ npx tsx scripts/proof-99273-completions-config.mjs

[PASS] resolved: catalog → Responses
[PASS] resolved: provider-level explicit completions  
[PASS] resolved: per-model explicit completions        ← THE FIX (was broken)
[PASS] transport: catalog → Responses
[PASS] transport: provider explicit → undefined
[PASS] transport: per-model explicit → undefined        ← THE FIX (was broken)

6/6 passed
```

### Data flow proof — per-model config survives normalization

```
User config:  {openai: {models: [{id: "gpt-5.5", api: "openai-completions"}]}}
  ↓ model.ts:747-757
  metadataOverrideModel.api = "openai-completions"      (per-model wins)
  resolvedModel.api = "openai-completions"
  ↓ normalizeResolvedModel callback
  hasExplicitOpenAICompletionsConfig(config, "gpt-5.5")
    → openaiCfg.models.some(m => m.id === "gpt-5.5" && m.api === "openai-completions")
    → TRUE → return ctx.model unchanged ✅
```

### Test regression

```
$ npx vitest run extensions/openai/openai-provider.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  45 passed (45)

$ npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/model.test.ts --run
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  246 passed (246)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/openai/openai-provider.ts
→ exit 0
```

### What was not tested

| Not tested | Why acceptable |
|------------|----------------|
| Real OpenAI endpoint E2E for each config level | The proof exercises the exact `normalizeResolvedModel` and `normalizeTransport` callback functions with their real production implementations — the same functions the gateway calls. Whether the API key works beyond this transport-normalization boundary is a separate concern from this predicate fix. |

## Root Cause

Two coupled problems in `extensions/openai/openai-provider.ts`:

1. **`shouldUseOpenAIResponsesTransport`**: A single-character logic error (`!==` for `===`) at L462 caused the early-return guard to execute the opposite of its intended behavior. But fixing this alone broke the transport path's catalog normalization.

2. **`normalizeOpenAITransport`**: Shared the same predicate, creating a coupling where the resolved-model path's catalog normalization and the transport path's per-request override used the same boolean function. After model resolution, the resolved `api` field carries no provenance bit — a per-model `api: "openai-completions"` config and the catalog default `api: "openai-completions"` are identical strings. The only way to distinguish them is to inspect the raw config.

target.title: fix(google-vertex): retry transient pre-stream failures and stale ADC
target.body:
## Summary

Vertex streaming requests currently fail the entire turn on two transient,
recoverable conditions:

1. **Pre-stream `429` / `503`** from the Vertex endpoint (rate limiting /
   backend unavailability), surfaced as a hard error before any SSE chunk is
   read.
2. **`401 UNAUTHENTICATED`** caused by a *stale cached ADC token* — the cache
   can outlive the upstream credential, which currently forces a restart to
   recover.

This PR adds narrowly-scoped, Vertex-only recovery for both:

- **Bounded retry for pre-stream `429`/`503`**: exponential backoff with jitter,
  honoring `Retry-After` (delta-seconds or HTTP-date) when present. Retries only
  happen **before** the first SSE chunk is parsed — once streaming has started we
  never retry, so a partially-streamed turn is never replayed.
- **Single `401` ADC retry**: on a Vertex `401 UNAUTHENTICATED` while using ADC,
  clear the cached token, re-resolve request headers, and retry exactly once.

Non-Vertex Google (Generative Language API / API-key) behavior is unchanged.

## Why

Vertex deployments periodically see `429`/`503` and post-rotation `401`s. Today
each one aborts a turn that would have succeeded on an immediate retry — the
single largest source of avoidable turn failures we observe against Vertex.

## Configuration (all optional, Vertex-only)

| Env var | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OPENCLAW_GOOGLE_VERTEX_STREAM_MAX_RETRIES` | `2` | Max pre-stream retries for 429/503 |
| `OPENCLAW_GOOGLE_VERTEX_STREAM_RETRY_BASE_DELAY_MS` | `250` | Backoff base |
| `OPENCLAW_GOOGLE_VERTEX_STREAM_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS` | `2000` | Backoff ceiling |

Defaults give ~2 quick retries; `MAX_RETRIES=0` fully disables the new
pre-stream retry path.

## Implementation notes

- New `fetchGooglePreStreamResponse()` wraps the pre-stream POST and is the only
  place the retry loop lives; both the non-Gemini-3 and Gemini-3 first-response
  paths route through it, so retry semantics are identical.
- `Retry-After` parsing supports both integer seconds and HTTP-date.
- The retry sleep is abort-aware (honors `options.signal`).
- A `clearGoogleVertexAdcTokenCache()` is exported from `vertex-adc.ts` for the
  401 path; the existing test-only `resetGoogleVertexAuthorizedUserTokenCacheForTest()`
  is kept as a thin alias for back-compat.
- Diagnostics go through `createSubsystemLogger("google-vertex/transport")`
  (`.debug`, gated by `OPENCLAW_LOG_LEVEL`) — no new stdout/stderr noise.

## Relationship to #61443

#61443 ("configurable retry for LLM provider API calls") adds a **generic**
provider-retry framework at the agent/provider layer (`src/infra/retry.ts`,
`src/agents/provider-retry.ts`) and wires it into `openai-transport-stream.ts`.
This change is **complementary**, not a duplicate:

- It does not reach the Google extension's own SSE transport
  (`extensions/google/transport-stream.ts`), where the Vertex pre-stream request
  is issued and parsed.
- The **401 stale-ADC recovery** here is auth-cache-specific: it must clear the
  cached token and re-resolve headers before retrying. A generic status-based
  retry would replay the *same* stale token and fail again.

If preferred, the 429/503 portion can later be expressed in terms of #61443's
framework once it lands; the 401-ADC portion stays Vertex-specific regardless.

## Test plan

`extensions/google/transport-stream.test.ts` — **66/66 pass on latest `main`**.
New cases:

- retries pre-stream `503`→`429`→success and returns the recovered stream;
- does **not** retry once an SSE chunk has arrived (malformed-JSON mid-stream
  still surfaces, partial content preserved);
- on `401 UNAUTHENTICATED`, clears the ADC cache, re-fetches the token, and
  retries once with the fresh `Authorization` header.

```
pnpm exec vitest run extensions/google/transport-stream.test.ts
# Test Files 1 passed (1) / Tests 66 passed (66)
```

Additionally validated against live `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` Vertex traffic in a
production deployment: real `streamGenerateContent` requests flow through the new
pre-stream wrapper and complete normally, confirming the path is non-breaking on
real traffic.

target.title: fix(daemon): detect and resolve dueling user+system systemd gateway units (#79375)
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #79375 — on Linux, after an upgrade a **user-scope** unit
(`~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service`) and a **system-scope** unit
(`/etc/systemd/system/openclaw-gateway.service`) can both exist and both try to
manage the gateway. They bind the same port and each instance's stale-process
detection SIGTERMs the other, producing an endless restart cascade.

Root cause: `findInstalledSystemdGatewayScope` checked the user path first and
**returned early**, so it could never surface that both scopes coexist — the
"dueling" condition was structurally invisible.

## What changed (three layers)

**1. Detection (`src/daemon/systemd.ts`)**
- New `findSystemdGatewayInstallation(env)` returns a discriminated union
  `{ kind: "none" | "user" | "system" | "dueling" }` reporting *every* installed
  scope without early-returning. Dueling requires **the same canonical unit
  name** in both scopes — a custom marker-owned system unit (an intentional
  separate gateway, e.g. a rescue bot) is **not** treated as a duplicate, so a
  legitimate user gateway is never auto-removed.
- `findInstalledSystemdGatewayScope` delegates to it while **preserving the
  exact user-first preference** its four lifecycle callers rely on (no behavior
  change for stop/restart/is-enabled/runtime).
- New `uninstallUserSystemdGatewayUnit` removes only the `$HOME` user unit (no
  root), mirroring `uninstallLegacySystemdUnits`. New pure
  `formatDuelingScopesWarning` helper.

**2. Doctor resolution (`src/commands/doctor-gateway-services.ts`)**
- `maybeResolveDuelingSystemdGatewayScopes` detects the dueling state and, after
  the existing confirm/policy gate, removes the redundant **user-scope** unit
  while keeping the root-installed **system-scope** unit authoritative — exactly
  the reporter's manual workaround. Declining or an externally-managed policy
  falls back to the existing cleanup hints. Wired into the doctor health flow.

**3. Startup guard (`src/cli/gateway-cli/run.ts`)**
- In service mode, only when a stale-kill actually happened, log a targeted
  remediation pointing at `openclaw doctor --fix`. Diagnostic only — the kill
  decision is unchanged; the lookup is skipped on clean starts.

The system-scope unit is never auto-removed (needs root); only a `sudo` hint is
offered for that direction. No new config keys.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** On Linux a user-scope and a system-scope
`openclaw-gateway.service` coexisting after upgrade bind the same port and
SIGTERM each other in an endless restart loop (#79375). After this patch the
doctor resolution path detects the dueling pair and removes the redundant
user-scope unit while keeping the system-scope unit, breaking the loop; a
custom-named system gateway is left untouched.

**Real environment tested:** Linux (kernel 6.17, Ubuntu 24.04), Node v26.0.0,
pnpm 11.2.2, real `systemd` with a root-created unit under
`/etc/systemd/system`. To avoid touching the host's production gateway the proof
is isolated via `OPENCLAW_SYSTEMD_UNIT=openclaw-proof-gateway`; the real
`openclaw-gateway` service stayed `active` throughout (verified after).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
```bash
# 1. build the patched tree
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=8192" npx tsdown

# 2. create a REAL root-owned system unit (isolated name, never enabled/started)
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/openclaw-proof-gateway.service <<'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=OpenClaw Proof (isolated)
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node x gateway --port 18789
UNIT

# 3. drive the COMPILED detector + the COMPILED user-unit uninstaller
#    (the same primitive doctor --fix calls) against real on-disk units
node /tmp/real-systemd-proof.mjs

# 4. clean up the isolated stubs
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/openclaw-proof-gateway.service
```

**Evidence after fix:** live `node`/`systemd` terminal output, redacted to the
isolated unit name:
```
[2] system unit present on disk: true
    detector -> {"kind":"dueling",
      "user":{"scope":"user","unitName":"openclaw-proof-gateway.service",
              "unitPath":".../.config/systemd/user/openclaw-proof-gateway.service"},
      "system":{"scope":"system","unitName":"openclaw-proof-gateway.service",
              "unitPath":"/etc/systemd/system/openclaw-proof-gateway.service"}}
    warning  -> detected BOTH a user-scope (...) and a system-scope (...) gateway
       unit bound to port 18789; they will SIGTERM each other in a restart loop.
       Run `openclaw doctor --fix` to remove the redundant user-scope unit, or:
       systemctl --user disable --now openclaw-proof-gateway.service && rm .../...
[3] running real uninstallUserSystemdGatewayUnit (user scope, no root):
    Removed user-scope systemd service: .../systemd/user/openclaw-proof-gateway.service
    result -> {"unitName":"openclaw-proof-gateway.service", ..., "removed":true}
    user unit still on disk?  false
    system unit still on disk? true
[4] post-cleanup detector -> {"kind":"system", ...}
```

**Observed result after fix:** the detector returns `dueling` only when both
scopes hold the **same canonical** unit; the real uninstaller removed exactly
the user-scope unit on disk and left the root-owned system unit in place, so a
subsequent detection reports `system` (loop resolved). The host's production
`openclaw-gateway.service` remained `active` the whole time. (Supplemental:
`npx tsdown` build complete; `oxlint` exit 0; `vitest` 132 passed incl. the
"custom marker-owned system gateway is not dueling" P1 safety test.)

**What was not tested:** a full interactive `openclaw doctor --fix` session
end-to-end (prompt → confirm → reinstall) against the **production** gateway, to
avoid disturbing the live service; instead the exact compiled resolution
primitive it invokes (`uninstallUserSystemdGatewayUnit`) was exercised against
real isolated systemd units, and the doctor flow wiring is covered by unit tests
(`maybeResolveDuelingSystemdGatewayScopes`: confirm / decline / external-policy /
single-scope / non-Linux). The WSL2-specific restart loop from the original
report was not live-reproduced.

target.title: feat(tui): classify every model as CLI / OAuth / API in /model picker
target.body:
## Summary

PR #91168 introduced a `runtimeLabel` field that only emitted `"CLI"` for models pinned to a CLI agentRuntime. Non-CLI models kept their old description (the human-readable model name), so users could not tell from the picker whether a given model is reached via subscription OAuth or a raw API key.

This PR extends the classification so every model in the `/model` picker carries a compact integration tag:

| Tag | Condition |
|---|---|
| `CLI` | `agentRuntime.id` pins the model to a CLI backend |
| `OAuth` | the canonical provider has an active OAuth credential |
| `API` | only an `api_key` / `token` credential is registered |
| (none) | no compatible profile / runtime resolved |

OAuth wins over API when both credentials exist for the same provider — users typically prefer the subscription path.

## Scope

- `src/agents/model-selection-cli.ts` — three new exports next to the existing `resolveModelRuntimeLabel`:
  - `classifyAuthCredentialIntegration(type)` — pure mapper
  - `resolveProviderAuthIntegrationLabel({provider, cfg, agentDir})` — reads `loadAuthProfileStoreWithoutExternalProfiles` (read-only, no external CLI sync) and walks the existing `resolveAuthProfileOrder`
  - `resolveModelIntegrationLabel({provider, modelId, cfg, agentDir})` — composite: prefers CLI, falls back to auth method
- `src/tui/embedded-backend.ts` — `listModels()` now resolves the default agent's dir and passes it to the helper.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/models-list-result.ts` — `buildPublicModelsListEntries` resolves `agentDir` once and threads it through `buildPublicModelsListEntry` (so the gateway response carries the same label).

Display-only — never used as a routing key. Statusline format stays `provider/model` (handled by PR #91177).

## Depends on

PR #91168 (introduces `runtimeLabel` + `resolveModelRuntimeLabel`). This PR replaces the helper call at the two existing call sites with the broader classifier.

## Real behavior proof
